title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
tagline: The numbers every engineer should know, and a repeatable recipe to size QPS, storage, and bandwidth in 5 minutes.
summary: The numbers to memorize + a recipe for QPS/storage/bandwidth.

paragraphs: Estimation turns a vague prompt into concrete numbers that *drive design decisions*. Whether you need 5 servers or 5,000, whether the data fits on one machine or needs sharding, whether you can cache everything in memory — all of this falls out of a few quick calculations. Interviewers ask for estimates to see if your architecture is grounded in reality, not hand-waving.

The goal is an *order of magnitude*, not precision. Round aggressively, use powers of ten, and state your assumptions out loud. Getting within ~2–3x of reality is a pass; spending 15 minutes on arithmetic is a fail.

blocks.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know (approx., orders of magnitude)

items.label: Round trip within same data center

blocks.title: The takeaways that matter
blocks.text: Memory is ~100,000x faster than disk and SSD is ~10–20x faster than HDD — *this is why we cache*. Cross-region round trips (~150 ms) are bounded by physics, not by faster hardware — *this is why we use CDNs and multi-region*. A same-DC round trip (~0.5 ms) is cheap, so chatty in-DC calls are usually fine; cross-region chattiness is not.

items.title: Start from users
items.detail: Get/assume Daily Active Users (DAU). Estimate actions per user per day (e.g., 2 posts, 50 reads).

items.title: Convert to QPS
items.detail: QPS = (DAU × actions/day) / 86,400 (seconds/day ≈ 100k, round to 10^5). Then **peak QPS ≈ 2–3× average** to handle bursts.

items.title: Split reads vs writes
items.detail: State the read:write ratio (often 10:1 to 100:1). It dictates caching/replication strategy.

items.title: Storage
items.detail: Per-item size × items/day × retention. Multiply by a replication factor (×3 is common).

items.title: Bandwidth
items.detail: QPS × average payload size = bytes/sec in and out. Media (images/video) dominates here.

items.title: Memory for cache
items.detail: Apply the 80/20 rule: cache the hot ~20% of data that serves ~80% of reads. Check it fits in RAM.

blocks.text: Shortcuts: 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10^5 s. 1 month ≈ 2.5M s. Always round to clean powers of ten and carry units. If a number is 'per day', divide by 10^5 to get per-second.

sections.title: Worked example: sizing a Twitter-like feed

paragraphs: Assume 200M DAU. Each user posts 2 tweets/day and reads their feed 50 times/day. A tweet is ~300 bytes of text (ignore media for now).

items.detail: 200M × 50 / 10^5 ≈ 100,000 reads/sec average → ~300,000/sec peak. Read:write ≈ 25:1 → heavy caching + precomputed feeds.
200M × 2 tweets × 300 B ≈ 120 GB/day of tweet text. Over a year ≈ 44 TB; ×3 replication ≈ 130 TB. Clearly needs sharding, not one box.
If each feed read returns ~10 tweets × 300 B = 3 KB → 100,000 × 3 KB ≈ 300 MB/s outbound (text only; media would dwarf this and belongs on a CDN).

blocks.text: Notice how the numbers *led* to architecture: 25:1 read:write → cache + precompute feeds (fan-out on write); 130 TB → shard the tweet store; media bandwidth → push to a CDN. That's the whole point — estimates justify your design, so tie each number to a decision.

cheatsheet: Estimation gives order-of-magnitude numbers that justify architecture — round hard, state assumptions.
1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10^5 s; peak QPS ≈ 2–3× average; replication factor ≈ ×3 for storage.
Memory ~100ns, SSD ~100µs, same-DC RTT ~0.5ms, disk seek ~10ms, US↔EU RTT ~150ms.
Memory ≫ SSD ≫ disk → cache; cross-region RTT is physics-bound → CDN/multi-region.
Recipe: DAU → actions → QPS (split read/write) → storage (size×count×retention×replication) → bandwidth → cache memory (80/20).

questions.prompt: Estimate the QPS and daily storage for a URL shortener with 100M new URLs created per day, average original URL 100 bytes, read:write ratio 100:1.
questions.hint: Convert per-day to per-second with /10^5; reads = 100× writes; storage = count × size × retention.
answer: Write QPS: 100M / 10^5 = ~1,000 writes/sec average, ~2,000–3,000/sec peak. Read QPS = 100× = ~100,000 reads/sec average, ~200,000–300,000/sec peak. The huge read skew screams 'cache the hot URLs aggressively'.

Storage: per record ≈ original URL (100 B) + short code + metadata ≈ ~500 B to be safe. 100M/day × 500 B = ~50 GB/day → ~18 TB/year, and we likely retain for years. With ×3 replication that's tens of TB — fine for a sharded key-value store, and the read path is dominated by cache hits.
keyPoints: Key-value store, sharded; reads served from cache
followUps: How many characters does the short code need to encode billions of URLs in base62?

questions.prompt: Why is 'memory is ~100,000x faster than disk' one of the most important numbers in system design?
questions.hint: What architectural pattern does this single fact justify?
answer: It's the entire justification for **caching** and for keeping hot data in RAM. If a value can be served from memory (~100 ns) instead of disk (~10 ms), you cut latency by orders of magnitude and offload the slow datastore. That's why we put Redis/Memcached in front of databases, hold indexes in memory, and design for high cache hit rates.

It also shapes data layout decisions: sequential disk/SSD access is far cheaper than random seeks, so systems batch and append (e.g., log-structured storage) rather than doing many random disk reads. The speed hierarchy — CPU cache > RAM > SSD > HDD > network/cross-region — drives where you want each piece of data to live.
keyPoints: Justifies caching / RAM for hot data
Memory ~100ns vs disk ~10ms = orders of magnitude
Also motivates sequential vs random access patterns
followUps: Given a 1 TB dataset and the 80/20 rule, how much cache RAM would you provision?
